terms.grammar: noun, second declension; the plural joca is Cicero’s
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.11.3: remōtō jocō tibi hoc amīcissimō animō praecipiō
Plaut. Poen. 541: equidem haec vōbīs dīxī per jocum
Traupman 101: jocō remōtō; per jocum, inter jocum
terms.comment: Per jocum or jocō, as a joke, in jest; the opposite is sēriō (see serious). Remōtō jocō and extrā jocum are “joking apart” (Lewis & Short). It also covers play and pastime generally (see fun).

terms.gloss: joke, jest; say as a joke
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.14.4: haec enim jocātus sum
Ter. Heaut. 729b: Atquī tū hanc jocārī crēdis?
terms.comment: Intransitive, or with what is said in jest: haec jocātus sum, I said this as a joke.
The laughable as a subject, as in Cicero’s and Quintilian’s chapters on wit; rīdiculī causā, for a laugh (Plaut. Am. 917). The adjective rīdiculus is funny, and also absurd (see funny).

phrases.latin: Nimis īrācundī estis: equidem haec vōbīs dīxī per jocum.
phrases.english: You’re far too touchy: I only said it as a joke.

phrases.latin: Heus tū, sī quid per jocum dīxī, nōlītō in sērium convertere.
phrases.english: Hey, if I said something as a joke, don’t turn it into something serious.
joking apart, he’s a nice man

phrases.latin: Atquī tū hanc jocārī crēdis? Faciet, nisi caveō.
phrases.english: And you think she’s joking? She’ll do it, unless I watch out.
